<p class="quiz-stem">What changed with the marginalist revolution at the end of the 19th century?</p>

<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q1-3"><span>a) The focus shifted from household management to the wealth of entire nations</span></label>

<label><input type="radio" autocomplete="off" name="q1-3"><span>c) The focus shifted from individual markets to economy-wide relationships</span></label>

</div>

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
**Question 1.1** (based on section 1.1)

An economist analyses why people marry and have children as a decision under scarcity of time, money and affection. Which understanding of economics does this reflect?

a) A substantivist understanding, because family life is part of the economy
b) A formal understanding, because economics is defined by its analytical approach, regardless of the subject matter
c) The understanding of classical political economy, because it concerns the reproduction of the working class
d) A feminist understanding, because it makes unpaid care work visible

**Question 1.2** (based on section 1.1)

Which of the following questions is typical of a substantivist understanding of economics?

a) How does a student best divide three free hours between studying, sport and friends?
b) How does a household maximize its utility given its budget?
c) How is bread produced and distributed, and who gets how much of societal wealth?
d) How do prices adjust until supply equals demand?

**Question 1.3** (based on section 1.1)

What changed with the marginalist revolution at the end of the 19th century?

a) The focus shifted from household management to the wealth of entire nations
b) The focus shifted from social classes, production and distribution to individual decisions on markets
c) The focus shifted from individual markets to economy-wide relationships
d) Economics was re-embedded in a moral and religious order

**Question 1.4** (based on section 1.1)

In ancient Greece, chrematistics, the accumulation of money, was regarded as the core of economics.

a) True
b) False

**Question 1.5** (based on section 1.3)

Which statement reflects a positivist view of economics?

a) Facts and values are often intertwined and cannot be clearly separated
b) Economics can describe the economy “as it is”, and positive statements can be clearly separated from normative ones
c) Different schools of thought can legitimately arrive at different interpretations of economic reality
d) Which questions researchers ask depends on their social and historical context

**Question 1.6** (based on section 1.4)

According to Ludwik Fleck, why do members of different thought collectives often have difficulty following each other’s arguments?

a) Because one collective usually has access to better data
b) Because they share a style of thought with its own concepts and methods, so they think, argue and understand in fundamentally different ways
c) Because thought collectives are organized along national language borders
d) Because only one collective can be scientifically correct at any time

**Question 1.7** (based on section 1.6)

How does sustainable economics, as understood in this script, position itself in the debate between green growth and post-growth?

a) It sides with green growth, because decoupling has been achieved worldwide
b) It sides with post-growth, because the economy must shrink
c) It first asks what ecological and social sustainability require and only then derives what role growth can or must play
d) It treats growth as irrelevant and focuses only on distribution

#### Answers and explanations {.unnumbered}

**1.1** b). Polanyi distinguishes two understandings. The formal one defines economics by an analytical approach (choice under scarcity, following Robbins) and applies it to any subject, including marriage. Gary Becker received the Nobel Memorial Prize for exactly this extension. A substantivist understanding would instead start from the economy as a subject matter: how people provide their means of subsistence.

**1.2** c). The substantivist understanding defines economics through its subject matter: how a society, in relation to its environment, provides the means of subsistence and distributes prosperity. The other three questions start from the analytical approach of choice under scarcity or the price mechanism, which is the formal understanding of the mainstream.

**1.3** b). Classical political economy (Smith, Ricardo, Marx) looked at whole economies, social classes and the distribution of the societal surplus. With Jevons, Menger and Walras, the starting point became the rational individual who maximizes utility or profit on markets. The shift from household to national wealth happened earlier (classical political economy), and the return to economy-wide questions came later with Keynes.

**1.4** False. False. Economics (oikos + nemein) meant household management embedded in politics and ethics, with the happy life (eudaimonia) as the ultimate goal. Chrematistics, which aimed at accumulating money, stood in sharp contrast to it and was rejected.

**1.5** b). Positivism assumes a reality governed by universal laws that can be described objectively, so economics should stick to positive statements (how the world is). The other options describe the critique: Putnam’s entanglement of facts and values and the constructivist view that knowledge is shaped by social contexts and perspectives.

**1.6** b). A thought collective shares a style of thought, a particular pair of “glasses” with its own concepts and methods. Collectives tend to resist change, and people from different collectives see the world through different glasses. Fleck stressed that knowledge always depends on values and contexts, which is why the script argues for pluralist economics.

**1.7** c). The polarization is didactically useful because it makes a real debate visible, but taken literally it is misleading. Sustainable economics does not start from a fixed answer (“more green growth” or “shrinkage”) but from the goals of economic activity: respecting ecological limits while enabling a good life for all.

:::
